Since 2001, this tiny storefront has been a pioneer in America's organic ice cream movement. Martin grew up right here in Fairfax, ran a restaurant over in Walnut Creek, then came back to Marin to raise his family and scoop something special. He builds around a hundred flavors on organic Straus Family Creamery cream, naming them for the land they come from — Marshall Melon, Tomales Strawberry, a vanilla honey-lavender with a genuine cult following.

Watch the waffle cones press up fresh, that warm aroma drifting down the sidewalk. Bring cash, bring patience — and enjoy every last lick.

spot.title: Good Earth Natural Foods

document.text:
Right here in Fairfax, this is Good Earth Natural Foods — an organic pioneer that's been feeding this town since 1969. It started small, over on Bolinas Road, back when finding organic rice was so tough that co-owner Mark Squire kept sacks of it stored under his bed. From those scrappy early days, Good Earth became one of the country's earliest champions of organic food, pushing growers to farm without chemical pesticides, blacklisting fraudulent suppliers, and holding standards so high they'd discontinue their best-selling chips the moment an organic version came along.

Today it fills this much larger home on Center Boulevard, built on the site of a former Albertsons, with wide, open aisles, vaulted ceilings, and redwood display cases. Yet for the families who've shopped here across generations, it still feels like coming home. Independently owned all these years, with a sister store in Mill Valley, Good Earth remains what it's always been — a true heart of this community.

Over the decades it changed with the times — split into smaller rooms in the early nineties, restored with better sound and picture, and eventually grown into the multi-screen house you see today, run now by Cinema West. In 2008 it even went solar, one of the first movie multiplexes in America to do so, with real butter and organic snacks at the counter. Krahling came up through California cooking's golden age, working the line at Joyce Goldstein's iconic Square One in San Francisco, then earning acclaim as chef at Butler's in Mill Valley, before betting everything on a big sunny room in her own home county. Ask a local where to take someone you love, and odds are they will just say the name: Insalata's.

document.text: At seventy-two eighty-two Sir Francis Drake Boulevard, a few doors from the Lagunitas market, is one of the stranger attractions in West Marin: a tea museum, open to the public on Saturday mornings, free of charge. It belongs to David Lee Hoffman, a tea importer whose business, the Phoenix Collection, sells loose-leaf white, green, black, oolong and aged pu-erh teas sourced directly from small growers in China. Hoffman became something of a cult figure after the documentary filmmaker Les Blank followed him into remote tea-growing mountains for the film All In This Tea, which premiered at the San Francisco International Film Festival in two thousand seven. The film follows him hunting for organic, hand-made leaf, talking terroir, and pressing for fair prices for the farmers who make it. The collection he brought back over decades lives here, in Lagunitas, in a village whose other claims to fame are a saloon, a general store, and a salmon run.

spot.title: The Eighteen Ninety-Two Farmhouse
spot.subtitle: A country acre of cottages at the edge of the seashore

locating.anchor: the old white farmhouse with cottages in its yard

document.text: Just before the village, a green acre with a two-story farmhouse marks the address nine nine seven zero Sir Francis Drake Boulevard. The house went up in eighteen ninety-two, the same year the new Catholic parish of Olema raised its first frame church along this boulevard, and it has been a farmstead ever since. Today it operates as Olema Cottages. The renovated farmhouse holds two guest suites, called the Farmer's Parlor and the Nest, and three freestanding cottages named Berry Vine, Sunflower and Cypress sit in private yards around it, with an outdoor sculpture garden and views across pastured horses to Inverness Ridge. It is half a mile from the national seashore entrance and a five-minute drive from Point Reyes Station. In a village where almost nothing is ever listed for sale, a working farmhouse from the eighteen nineties that rents by the night is about as close as Olema gets to a real estate market.

spot.title: Eighty Percent of a Lodge
spot.subtitle: A nineteen eighty-eight inn, a four-million-dollar makeover, and a new name

locating.anchor: the big shingled lodge on lawns at the crossroads

document.text: The shingled lodge on four acres of lawn at the crossroads was built in nineteen eighty-eight as a bed and breakfast, and for thirty years travelers knew it as the Point Reyes Seashore Lodge, later the Lodge at Point Reyes. In the fall of twenty eighteen, Mosaic Hotel Group, a division of the San Rafael company Palisades Hospitality Group led by Tim Harmon, bought an eighty percent interest in the property. The new owners spent more than four million dollars on renovations, brought in chef Justin Bruckert, and in March twenty nineteen relaunched the place as Olema House, with twenty-four rooms spread across cottages, bi-level suites and guest rooms. The tavern on the grounds, now called Due West, occupies a building the hotel dates to eighteen sixty-five. The pitch was an eclectic bohemian hideaway for outdoor adventurers, which is a long way from the artichoke fields and cattle that surrounded this junction within living memory.

spot.title: The Gamekeeper's House
spot.subtitle: A nineteen ten redwood cottage from the hunting lodge days

locating.anchor: the small wooden house at the corner of Bear Valley Road

document.text: At the corner where Bear Valley Road leaves Highway One stands a modest two-story house that was built around nineteen ten, when this was still Shafter estate land. The Shafters ran the Bear Valley Lodge up the valley as a hunting destination for wealthy San Franciscans, who came out to shoot deer, mountain lion and, in the earlier years, bear. The lodge needed a gamekeeper, and this was his house. It was built entirely of the best redwood, walls, ceilings and floors alike, and the original redwood gutter, roughly a century old, still carries rain off the roof. The cottage went up as Olema was fading. The village had once had two churches, seven bars, a race track and two hotels, serving the traffic between the redwood forests and the port at Bolinas, but the eighteen seventy-four railway to Point Reyes Station drained its trade northward. Today the gamekeeper's house takes overnight guests as Bear Valley Cottage.

spot.title: The Barber Chair in the Window
spot.subtitle: The West Coast's oldest saloon, seen across the water

locating.anchor: the cluster of waterfront buildings across the lagoon at the foot of the Bolinas bluff

document.text: Across the water, where the far shore of the lagoon meets the bluff, the waterfront buildings of Bolinas line Wharf Road, and one of them has been pouring drinks since eighteen fifty-one. Smiley's Schooner Saloon was built for Captain Isaac Morgan when Wharf Road was a working port and schooners shuttled lumber and produce to San Francisco. It has been called the oldest continuously operating saloon on the West Coast. During Prohibition a barber named Marion Bettencourt ran the place, and he installed his barber's chair in the front window so that anyone passing by saw a respectable barbershop. The bar kept working behind it, and local legend holds that Smiley's never closed a single day of the dry years. In nineteen fifty-five an Italian immigrant and former San Francisco restaurateur, Ismaele Bianchini, known to everyone as Smiley, bought it, added a bait shop, and gave it the name it carries today. The hotel rooms upstairs still rent by the night.

spot.title: Lunch at the Lifeguard Tower
spot.subtitle: A nineteen sixties beach building, a ten-year contract, and a long dark spell

locating.anchor: the low lifeguard building between the parking lot and the sand

document.text: The low building between the parking lot and the sand at the south end of the beach is the lifeguard tower, and it shares its walls with the only place to buy lunch on the beach itself. The National Park Service says the structure dates from the nineteen sixties, and it serves a beach that draws about a million visitors a year, the only staffed swimming beach in the whole Golden Gate National Recreation Area. The snack window has been run since twenty fourteen by a Mill Valley restaurateur who named it the Siren Canteen. In December twenty eighteen the park chose her for a new ten-year contract beginning March first, twenty nineteen, then closed the building for a full rehabilitation because the grill was failing and the kitchen needed rebuilding. During the federal shutdown early that year she wrote personal checks to keep the trash pickup and restrooms going while the rangers were furloughed. After several summers dark, the canteen was slated to reopen in June of twenty twenty-five.

spot.title: The Only Grocery in Town
spot.subtitle: The corner of Calle del Mar, where the village does its shopping

locating.anchor: the market on the corner of Calle del Mar

document.text: The corner where Calle del Mar meets Highway One is the working center of the village, and the store on it, Stinson Beach Market, is the only grocery in town. It is small but not tiny, locally owned, and stocked on the has-everything model of a beach town with no other option: produce and meat, wine and beer, ice, sunscreen, firewood, and sandwiches to carry down to the sand. For residents it is simply the store. For the day visitors who pour in on a summer weekend it is the last stop before the beach, and the little lot on this corner fills early. Calle del Mar itself does not run toward the water. It climbs from this corner into the hillside neighborhood of Buena Vista and Belvedere, first as a lane and then as a public stairway. From here south, Highway One leaves the village behind and there is nothing for sale of any kind along the cliffs past Steep Ravine.

spot.title: Pelican Inn and English Inn Architecture
spot.subtitle: Local history

document.text: Near the Muir Beach approach, a whitewashed inn compresses centuries of English architectural taste into a building from the 1970s. The Pelican Inn was designed to evoke a sixteenth-century country inn, with a slate roof, low beams, wood paneling and a small bar. Inside, seven bedrooms carry the theme through English antiques and canopy beds. There is even a snug: a separate sitting room reserved for overnight guests, with a fireplace, books and games. Its carefully assembled appearance is part of modern Muir Beach's history, just inland from the ocean.
